Kennedy exchanged two sets of letters with Khrushchev, to no avail.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993390_184-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993390-184">&#91;183&#93;</a></sup> United Nations (UN) Secretary General <a href="/wiki/U_Thant" title="U Thant">U Thant</a> requested both parties to reverse their decisions and enter a cooling-off period. Khrushchev agreed, but Kennedy did not.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993403_185-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993403-185">&#91;184&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>One Soviet-flagged ship was stopped and boarded. On October 28, Khrushchev agreed to dismantle the missile sites, subject to UN inspections.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993426_186-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993426-186">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup> The U.S. publicly promised never to invade Cuba and privately agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Italy and Turkey, which were by then obsolete and had been supplanted by submarines equipped with <a href="/wiki/UGM-27_Polaris" title="UGM-27 Polaris">UGM-27 Polaris</a> missiles.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKenney2000184–186_187-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKenney2000184–186-187">&#91;186&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>This crisis brought the world closer to nuclear war than at any point before or after. It is considered that "the humanity" of both Khrushchev and Kennedy prevailed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKenney2000189_188-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKenney2000189-188">&#91;187&#93;</a></sup> The crisis improved the image of American willpower and the president's credibility. Kennedy's approval rating increased from 66% to 77% immediately thereafter.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993425_189-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993425-189">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Latin_America_and_communism">Latin America and communism</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_John_F._Kennedy_administration#Latin_America" title="Foreign policy of the John F. Kennedy administration">Foreign policy of the John F. Kennedy administration §&#160;Latin America</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Kennedy_-_signing_Cuba_Quarantine_Proclamation.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/President_Kennedy_-_signing_Cuba_Quarantine_Proclamation.jpg/190px-President_Kennedy_-_signing_Cuba_Quarantine_Proclamation.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="240" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/President_Kennedy_-_signing_Cuba_Quarantine_Proclamation.jpg/285px-President_Kennedy_-_signing_Cuba_Quarantine_Proclamation.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/President_Kennedy_-_signing_Cuba_Quarantine_Proclamation.jpg/380px-President_Kennedy_-_signing_Cuba_Quarantine_Proclamation.jpg 2x" data-file-width="666" data-file-height="842" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy signs the <a href="/wiki/Cuban_Missile_Crisis" title="Cuban Missile Crisis">Proclamation for Interdiction of the Delivery of Offensive Weapons to Cuba</a> in the Oval Office, October 23, 1962.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Believing that "those who make peaceful revolution impossible, will make violent revolution inevitable,"<sup id="cite_ref-190" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-190">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-191" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-191">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy sought to contain the perceived threat of communism in Latin America by establishing the <a href="/wiki/Alliance_for_Progress" title="Alliance for Progress">Alliance for Progress</a>, which sent aid to some countries and sought greater human rights standards in the region.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESchlesinger2002788,_789_192-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger2002788,_789-192">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup> He worked closely with <a href="/wiki/Governor_of_Puerto_Rico" title="Governor of Puerto Rico">Puerto Rican Governor</a> <a href="/wiki/Luis_Mu%C3%B1oz_Mar%C3%ADn" title="Luis Muñoz Marín">Luis Muñoz Marín</a> for the development of the Alliance of Progress and began working to further <a href="/wiki/Puerto_Rico" title="Puerto Rico">Puerto Rico</a>'s autonomy.
</p><p>The Eisenhower administration, through the CIA, had begun formulating plans to assassinate Castro in Cuba and <a href="/wiki/Rafael_Trujillo" title="Rafael Trujillo">Rafael Trujillo</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Dominican_Republic" title="Dominican Republic">Dominican Republic</a>. When Kennedy took office, he privately instructed the CIA that any plan must include <a href="/wiki/Plausible_deniability" title="Plausible deniability">plausible deniability</a> by the U.S. His public position was in opposition.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993140–142_193-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993140–142-193">&#91;192&#93;</a></sup> In June 1961, the Dominican Republic's leader was assassinated; in the days following, Undersecretary of State <a href="/wiki/Chester_Bowles" class="mw-redirect" title="Chester Bowles">Chester Bowles</a> led a cautious reaction by the nation. Robert Kennedy, who saw an opportunity for the U.S., called Bowles "a gutless bastard" to his face.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993152_194-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993152-194">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Southeast_Asia">Southeast Asia</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Laotian_Civil_War" title="Laotian Civil War">Laotian Civil War</a>, <a href="/wiki/Taylor-Rostow_Report" title="Taylor-Rostow Report">Taylor-Rostow Report</a>, <a href="/wiki/1963_South_Vietnamese_coup" class="mw-redirect" title="1963 South Vietnamese coup">1963 South Vietnamese coup</a>, <a href="/wiki/Arrest_and_assassination_of_Ngo_Dinh_Diem" title="Arrest and assassination of Ngo Dinh Diem">Arrest and assassination of Ngo Dinh Diem</a>, <a href="/wiki/Reaction_to_the_1963_South_Vietnamese_coup" class="mw-redirect" title="Reaction to the 1963 South Vietnamese coup">Reaction to the 1963 South Vietnamese coup</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cable_243" title="Cable 243">Cable 243</a>, <a href="/wiki/Buddhist_crisis" title="Buddhist crisis">Buddhist crisis</a>, <a href="/wiki/Th%C3%ADch_Qu%E1%BA%A3ng_%C4%90%E1%BB%A9c" title="Thích Quảng Đức">Thích Quảng Đức</a>, <a href="/wiki/X%C3%A1_L%E1%BB%A3i_Pagoda_raids" title="Xá Lợi Pagoda raids">Xá Lợi Pagoda raids</a>, <a href="/wiki/Krulak_Mendenhall_mission" class="mw-redirect" title="Krulak Mendenhall mission">Krulak Mendenhall mission</a>, and <a href="/wiki/McNamara_Taylor_mission" class="mw-redirect" title="McNamara Taylor mission">McNamara Taylor mission</a></div>
<p>As a U.S. Congressman in 1951, Kennedy became fascinated with Vietnam after visiting the area as part of a big fact-finding mission to Asia and the Middle East, even stressing in a subsequent radio address that he strongly favored "check[ing] the southern drive of communism."<sup id="cite_ref-195" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-195">&#91;194&#93;</a></sup> As a U.S. senator in 1956, Kennedy publicly advocated for greater U.S. involvement in Vietnam.<sup id="cite_ref-196" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-196">&#91;195&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-197" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-197">&#91;196&#93;</a></sup> When briefing Kennedy, Eisenhower emphasized that the communist threat in Southeast Asia required priority; Eisenhower considered <a href="/wiki/Laos" title="Laos">Laos</a> to be "the cork in the bottle" regarding the regional threat. In March 1961, Kennedy voiced a change in policy from supporting a "free" Laos to a "neutral" Laos, indicating privately that <a href="/wiki/Vietnam" title="Vietnam">Vietnam</a>, and not Laos, should be deemed America's tripwire for communism's spread in the area.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves199375_198-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves199375-198">&#91;197&#93;</a></sup> In May, he dispatched Lyndon Johnson to meet with South Vietnamese President <a href="/wiki/Ngo_Dinh_Diem" title="Ngo Dinh Diem">Ngo Dinh Diem</a>. Johnson assured Diem more aid to mold a fighting force that could resist the communists.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKarnow1991230,_268_199-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarnow1991230,_268-199">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy announced a change of policy from support to partnership with Diem to defeat of communism in <a href="/wiki/South_Vietnam" title="South Vietnam">South Vietnam</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993119_200-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993119-200">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During his presidency, Kennedy continued policies that provided political, economic, and military support to the governments of South Korea and South Vietnam:<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDunniganNofi1999257_201-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunniganNofi1999257-201">&#91;200&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-JFKennedy1962_202-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-JFKennedy1962-202">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<blockquote><p>We have one-million Americans today serving outside the United-States. There's no other country in history that's carried this kind of a burden. Other countries have had forces serving outside their own country, but for conquest. We have two divisions in South-Korea, not to control South-Korea, but to defend it. We have a lot of Americans in South Vietnam. Well, no other country in the world has ever done that since the beginning of the world; <a href="/wiki/Greece" title="Greece">Greece</a>, Rome, <a href="/wiki/Napoleon" title="Napoleon">Napoleon</a>, and all the rest, always had conquest. We have a million men outside, and they try to defend these countries.<sup id="cite_ref-JFKennedy1962_202-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-JFKennedy1962-202">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Kennedy_1961_CIA_map_(30253020214).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/President_Kennedy_1961_CIA_map_%2830253020214%29.jpg/220px-President_Kennedy_1961_CIA_map_%2830253020214%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="176" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/President_Kennedy_1961_CIA_map_%2830253020214%29.jpg/330px-President_Kennedy_1961_CIA_map_%2830253020214%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/President_Kennedy_1961_CIA_map_%2830253020214%29.jpg/440px-President_Kennedy_1961_CIA_map_%2830253020214%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1277" data-file-height="1024" /></a><figcaption>News conference, March 23, 1961</figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Viet_Cong" title="Viet Cong">Viet Cong</a> began assuming a predominant presence in late 1961, initially seizing the provincial capital of Phuoc Vinh.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993240_203-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993240-203">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup> After a mission to Vietnam in October, presidential adviser General <a href="/wiki/Maxwell_D._Taylor" title="Maxwell D. Taylor">Maxwell D. Taylor</a> and <a href="/wiki/Deputy_National_Security_Adviser" class="mw-redirect" title="Deputy National Security Adviser">Deputy National Security Adviser</a> <a href="/wiki/Walt_Rostow" title="Walt Rostow">Walt Rostow</a> <a href="/wiki/Taylor-Rostow_Report" title="Taylor-Rostow Report">recommended</a> the deployment of 6,000 to 8,000 U.S. combat troops to Vietnam.<sup id="cite_ref-204" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-204">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup>  Kennedy increased the number of military advisers and <a href="/wiki/U.S._Special_Forces" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Special Forces">special forces</a> in the area, from 11,000 in 1962 to 16,000 by late 1963, but he was reluctant to order a full-scale deployment of troops.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993242_205-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993242-205">&#91;204&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-206" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-206">&#91;205&#93;</a></sup> However, Kennedy, who was wary about the region's successful war of independence against France, was also eager to not give the impression to the Vietnamese people that the United States was acting as the region's new colonizer, even stating in his journal at one point that the United States was "more and more becoming colonists in the minds of the people."<sup id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-207">&#91;206&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In late 1961, Kennedy sent <a href="/wiki/Roger_Hilsman" title="Roger Hilsman">Roger Hilsman</a>, then director of the State Department's <a href="/wiki/Bureau_of_Intelligence_and_Research" title="Bureau of Intelligence and Research">Bureau of Intelligence and Research</a>, to assess the situation in Vietnam. There, Hilsman met Sir <a href="/wiki/Robert_Grainger_Ker_Thompson" title="Robert Grainger Ker Thompson">Robert Grainger Ker Thompson</a>, head of the British Advisory Mission to South Vietnam, and the <a href="/wiki/Strategic_Hamlet_Program" title="Strategic Hamlet Program">Strategic Hamlet Program</a> was formed. It was approved by Kennedy and South Vietnam President <a href="/wiki/Ngo_Dinh_Diem" title="Ngo Dinh Diem">Ngo Dinh Diem</a>. It was implemented in early 1962 and involved some forced relocation, village internment, and segregation of rural South Vietnamese into new communities where the peasantry would be isolated from communist insurgents. It was hoped that these new communities would provide security for the peasants and strengthen the tie between them and the central government. By November 1963, the program waned and officially ended in 1964.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETucker20111070_208-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETucker20111070-208">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On January 18, 1962, Kennedy formally authorized escalated involvement when he signed the National Security Action Memorandum&#160;– "Subversive Insurgency (War of Liberation)".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993281_209-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993281-209">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup> "<a href="/wiki/Operation_Ranch_Hand" title="Operation Ranch Hand">Operation Ranch Hand</a>", a large-scale aerial defoliation effort, began on the roadsides of South Vietnam initiating the use of the herbicide <a href="/wiki/Agent_Orange" title="Agent Orange">Agent Orange</a> on foliage and to combat <a href="/wiki/Guerrilla_warfare" title="Guerrilla warfare">guerrilla defendants</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993259_210-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993259-210">&#91;209&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-211" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-211">&#91;210&#93;</a></sup> Initially under consideration as to whether or not the use of the chemical would violate the <a href="/wiki/Geneva_Convention" class="mw-redirect" title="Geneva Convention">Geneva Convention</a>, the application would be justified by the administration by <a href="/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State" title="United States Secretary of State">Secretary of State</a> <a href="/wiki/Dean_Rusk" title="Dean Rusk">Dean Rusk</a> who argued to Kennedy that "[t]he use of defoliant does not violate any rule of international law concerning the conduct of chemical warfare and is an accepted tactic of war. Precedent has been established by the British during the emergency in Malaya in their use of aircraft for destroying crops by chemical spraying".<sup id="cite_ref-212" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-212">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup> Depending on which assessment Kennedy accepted (Department of Defense or State), there had been zero or modest progress in countering the increase in communist aggression in return for an expanded U.S. involvement.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993283_213-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993283-213">&#91;212&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_meets_with_Secretary_of_Defense._President_Kennedy,_Secretary_McNamara._White_House,_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_194244.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/President_meets_with_Secretary_of_Defense._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_McNamara._White_House%2C_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_194244.jpg/220px-President_meets_with_Secretary_of_Defense._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_McNamara._White_House%2C_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_194244.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="220" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/President_meets_with_Secretary_of_Defense._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_McNamara._White_House%2C_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_194244.jpg/330px-President_meets_with_Secretary_of_Defense._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_McNamara._White_House%2C_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_194244.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/President_meets_with_Secretary_of_Defense._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_McNamara._White_House%2C_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_194244.jpg/440px-President_meets_with_Secretary_of_Defense._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_McNamara._White_House%2C_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_194244.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2700" data-file-height="2700" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy and Secretary of Defense <a href="/wiki/Robert_McNamara" title="Robert McNamara">Robert McNamara</a>, 1962</figcaption></figure>
<p>In April 1963, Kennedy assessed the situation in Vietnam, saying, "We don't have a prayer of staying in Vietnam. Those people hate us. They are going to throw our asses out of there at any point. But I can't give up that territory to the communists and get the American people to re-elect me."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993484_214-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993484-214">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On August 21, just as the new U.S. Ambassador <a href="/wiki/Henry_Cabot_Lodge_Jr." title="Henry Cabot Lodge Jr.">Henry Cabot Lodge Jr.</a> arrived, Diem and his brother <a href="/wiki/Ngo_Dinh_Nhu" class="mw-redirect" title="Ngo Dinh Nhu">Ngo Dinh Nhu</a> ordered South Vietnam forces, funded and trained by the CIA, to quell Buddhist demonstrations. The crackdowns heightened expectations of a coup d'état to remove Diem with (or perhaps by) his brother, Nhu.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993558_215-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993558-215">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup> Lodge was instructed to try getting Diem and Nhu to step down and leave the country. Diem would not listen to Lodge.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993559_216-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993559-216">&#91;215&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Cable_243" title="Cable 243">Cable 243</a> (DEPTEL 243) followed, dated August 24, declaring that Washington would no longer tolerate Nhu's actions, and Lodge was ordered to pressure Diem to remove Nhu.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993562–563_217-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993562–563-217">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup> Lodge concluded that the only option was to get the South Vietnamese generals to overthrow Diem and Nhu.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993573_218-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993573-218">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup> At week's end, orders were sent to Saigon and throughout Washington to "destroy all coup cables".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993577_219-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993577-219">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup> At the same time, the first formal anti-Vietnam war sentiment was expressed by U.S. clergy from the Ministers' Vietnam Committee.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993560_220-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993560-220">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>A White House meeting in September was indicative of the different ongoing appraisals; Kennedy received updated assessments after <a href="/wiki/Krulak_Mendenhall_mission" class="mw-redirect" title="Krulak Mendenhall mission">personal inspections on the ground</a> by the Departments of Defense (General <a href="/wiki/Victor_Krulak" class="mw-redirect" title="Victor Krulak">Victor Krulak</a>) and State (<a href="/wiki/Joseph_Mendenhall" class="mw-redirect" title="Joseph Mendenhall">Joseph Mendenhall</a>). Krulak said that the military fight against the communists was progressing and being won, while Mendenhall stated that the country was civilly being lost to any U.S. influence. Kennedy reacted, asking, "Did you two gentlemen visit the same country?" Kennedy was unaware that both men were so much at odds that they did not speak to each other on the return flight.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993595_221-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993595-221">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In October 1963, Kennedy appointed Defense Secretary McNamara and General <a href="/wiki/Maxwell_D._Taylor" title="Maxwell D. Taylor">Maxwell D. Taylor</a> to a Vietnamese mission in another effort to synchronize the information and formulation of policy. The objective of the <a href="/wiki/McNamara_Taylor_mission" class="mw-redirect" title="McNamara Taylor mission">McNamara Taylor mission</a> "emphasized the importance of getting to the bottom of the differences in reporting from U.S. representatives in Vietnam".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993602_222-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993602-222">&#91;221&#93;</a></sup> In meetings with McNamara, Taylor, and Lodge, Diem again refused to agree to governing measures, helping to dispel McNamara's previous optimism about Diem.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993609_223-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993609-223">&#91;222&#93;</a></sup> Taylor and McNamara were enlightened by Vietnam's vice president, <a href="/wiki/Nguyen_Ngoc_Tho" class="mw-redirect" title="Nguyen Ngoc Tho">Nguyen Ngoc Tho</a> (choice of many to succeed Diem), who in detailed terms obliterated Taylor's information that the military was succeeding in the countryside.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993610_224-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993610-224">&#91;223&#93;</a></sup> At Kennedy's insistence, the mission report contained a recommended schedule for troop withdrawals: 1,000 by year's end and complete withdrawal in 1965, something the NSC considered to be a "strategic fantasy".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993613_225-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993613-225">&#91;224&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In late October, intelligence wires again reported that a coup against the Diem government was afoot. The source, Vietnamese General <a href="/wiki/Duong_Van_Minh" class="mw-redirect" title="Duong Van Minh">Duong Van Minh</a> (also known as "Big Minh"), wanted to know the U.S. position. Kennedy instructed Lodge to offer covert assistance to the coup, excluding assassination.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993617_226-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993617-226">&#91;225&#93;</a></sup> On November 1, 1963, South Vietnamese generals, led by "Big Minh", <a href="/wiki/1963_South_Vietnamese_coup" class="mw-redirect" title="1963 South Vietnamese coup">overthrew the Diem government</a>, arresting <a href="/wiki/Arrest_and_assassination_of_Ngo_Dinh_Diem" title="Arrest and assassination of Ngo Dinh Diem">and then killing Diem and Nhu</a>. Kennedy was shocked by the deaths.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993650_227-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993650-227">&#91;226&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>News of the coup led to renewed confidence initially—both in America and in South Vietnam—that the war might be won.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993651_228-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993651-228">&#91;227&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/McGeorge_Bundy" title="McGeorge Bundy">McGeorge Bundy</a> drafted a National Security Action Memo to present to Kennedy upon his return from Dallas. It reiterated the resolve to fight communism in Vietnam, with increasing military and economic aid and expansion of operations into Laos and Cambodia. Before leaving for Dallas, Kennedy told <a href="/wiki/Michael_Forrestal" title="Michael Forrestal">Michael Forrestal</a> that "after the first of the year&#160;... [he wanted] an in depth study of every possible option, including how to get out of there&#160;... to review this whole thing from the bottom to the top". Asked what he thought Kennedy meant, Forrestal said, "It was devil's advocate stuff."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993660_229-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993660-229">&#91;228&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Kennedy_American_University_Commencement_Address_June_10,_1963.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/President_Kennedy_American_University_Commencement_Address_June_10%2C_1963.jpg/220px-President_Kennedy_American_University_Commencement_Address_June_10%2C_1963.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="214" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/President_Kennedy_American_University_Commencement_Address_June_10%2C_1963.jpg/330px-President_Kennedy_American_University_Commencement_Address_June_10%2C_1963.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/President_Kennedy_American_University_Commencement_Address_June_10%2C_1963.jpg/440px-President_Kennedy_American_University_Commencement_Address_June_10%2C_1963.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2632" data-file-height="2562" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy delivers the <a href="/wiki/Commencement_speech" title="Commencement speech">commencement speech</a> at <a href="/wiki/American_University" title="American University">American University</a>, June 10, 1963.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Historians disagree on whether the <a href="/wiki/Vietnam_War" title="Vietnam War">Vietnam War</a> would have escalated if Kennedy had not been assassinated and had won re-election in 1964.<sup id="cite_ref-230" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-230">&#91;229&#93;</a></sup> Fueling the debate were statements made by Secretary of Defense McNamara in the 2003 documentary film <i><a href="/wiki/The_Fog_of_War" title="The Fog of War">The Fog of War</a></i> that Kennedy was strongly considering pulling the United States out of Vietnam after the 1964 election.<sup id="cite_ref-231" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-231">&#91;230&#93;</a></sup> The film also contains a tape recording of Lyndon Johnson stating that Kennedy was planning to withdraw, a position with which Johnson disagreed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBlightLang2005276_232-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlightLang2005276-232">&#91;231&#93;</a></sup> Conversely, in 2008, Kennedy administration <a href="/wiki/White_House_Counsel" title="White House Counsel">White House Counsel</a> and speechwriter <a href="/wiki/Ted_Sorensen" title="Ted Sorensen">Ted Sorensen</a> wrote, "I would like to believe that Kennedy would have found a way to withdraw all American instructors and advisors [from Vietnam]. But even someone who knew JFK as well as I did can't be certain, because I do not believe he knew in his last weeks what he was going to do." Sorensen added that, in his opinion, Vietnam "was the only foreign policy problem handed off by JFK to his successor in no better, and possibly worse, shape than it was when he inherited it."<sup id="cite_ref-233" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-233">&#91;232&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>At the time of Kennedy's death, no final policy decision was made with respect to Vietnam.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMatthews2011393,_394_234-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews2011393,_394-234">&#91;233&#93;</a></sup> By November 1963, there were 16,000 American military personnel in South Vietnam, up from Eisenhower's 900 advisors.<sup id="cite_ref-235" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-235">&#91;234&#93;</a></sup> In the aftermath of the aborted coup in September 1963, the Kennedy administration reevaluated its policies in South Vietnam. Kennedy rejected both the full-scale deployment of ground soldiers, but also rejected the total withdrawal of U.S. forces from the country.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGiglio2006265–266_236-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiglio2006265–266-236">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy had signed National Security Action Memorandum (NSAM) 263, dated October 11, which ordered the withdrawal of 1,000 military personnel by year's end, and the bulk of them out by 1965.<sup id="cite_ref-NSAM_263_237-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NSAM_263-237">&#91;236&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDallek2003680_238-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek2003680-238">&#91;237&#93;</a></sup> Such an action would have been a policy reversal, but Kennedy was publicly moving in a less hawkish direction since his speech on world peace at <a href="/wiki/American_University" title="American University">American University</a> on June 10, 1963.<sup id="cite_ref-AmUniv_239-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AmUniv-239">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup> After Kennedy's assassination, President Johnson signed NSAM 273 on November 26, 1963. It reversed Kennedy's decision to withdraw 1,000 troops and reaffirmed the policy of assistance to the South Vietnamese.<sup id="cite_ref-240" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-240">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-241" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-241">&#91;240&#93;</a></sup> U.S. involvement in the region escalated until his successor Lyndon Johnson directly deployed regular U.S. military forces for fighting the <a href="/wiki/Vietnam_War" title="Vietnam War">Vietnam War</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKarnow1991339,_343_242-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarnow1991339,_343-242">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-243" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-243">&#91;242&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="American_University_speech">American University speech</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1134653256"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096940132"><div class="side-box side-box-right listen noprint"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1126788409">
<div class="side-box-flex">
<div class="side-box-image"><figure class="mw-halign-center" typeof="mw:File"><span><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/50px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png" decoding="async" width="50" height="50" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/75px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/100px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="160" data-file-height="160" /></span><figcaption></figcaption></figure></div>
<div class="side-box-text plainlist"><div class="haudio">
<div class="listen-file-header"><a href="/wiki/File:Jfk_American_University_4654_06-10-63.ogg" title="File:Jfk American University 4654 06-10-63.ogg"><i>World Peace</i> Speech</a></div>
<div><span typeof="mw:File"><span><audio id="mwe_player_5" controls="" preload="none" class="mw-file-element" width="232" style="width:232px;" data-durationhint="1607" data-mwtitle="Jfk_American_University_4654_06-10-63.ogg" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/b/b5/Jfk_American_University_4654_06-10-63.ogg/Jfk_American_University_4654_06-10-63.ogg.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" data-title="MP3" data-shorttitle="MP3" data-transcodekey="mp3" data-width="0" data-height="0" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b5/Jfk_American_University_4654_06-10-63.ogg" type="audio/ogg; codecs=&quot;vorbis&quot;" data-title="Original Ogg file (130 kbps)" data-shorttitle="Ogg source" data-width="0" data-height="0" /></audio></span></span></div>
<div class="description">Speech from <a href="/wiki/American_University" title="American University">American University</a> by John F. Kennedy, June 10, 1963 (duration 26:47)</div></div></div></div>
<div class="side-box-abovebelow"><hr /><i class="selfreference">Problems playing this file? See <a href="/wiki/Help:Media" title="Help:Media">media help</a>.</i></div>
</div>
<p>On June 10, 1963, Kennedy, at the high point of his rhetorical powers,<sup id="cite_ref-244" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-244">&#91;243&#93;</a></sup> delivered the <a href="/wiki/American_University_speech" title="American University speech">commencement address at American University</a> in Washington, D.C. Also known as "A Strategy of Peace", not only did Kennedy outline a plan to curb nuclear arms, but he also "laid out a hopeful, yet realistic route for world peace at a time when the U.S. and Soviet Union faced the potential for an escalating nuclear arms race."<sup id="cite_ref-245" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-245">&#91;244&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy wished:
</p>
<blockquote><p>to discuss a topic on which too often ignorance abounds and the truth is too rarely perceived—yet it is the most important topic on earth: world peace&#160;... I speak of peace because of the new face of war ... in an age when a singular nuclear weapon contains ten times the explosive force delivered by all the allied forces in the Second World War&#160;... an age when the deadly poisons produced by a nuclear exchange would be carried by wind and air and soil and seed to the far corners of the globe and to generations yet unborn&#160;... I speak of peace, therefore, as the necessary rational end of rational men&#160;... world peace, like community peace, does not require that each man love his neighbor—it requires only that they live together in mutual tolerance&#160;... our problems are man-made—therefore they can be solved by man. And man can be as big as he wants.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993513–514_246-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993513–514-246">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>Kennedy also made two announcements: 1.) that the Soviets had expressed a desire to negotiate a nuclear test ban treaty, and 2.) that the U.S. had postponed planned atmospheric tests.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993514_247-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993514-247">&#91;246&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="West_Berlin_speech">West Berlin speech</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:JFKBerlinSpeech.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/JFKBerlinSpeech.jpg/220px-JFKBerlinSpeech.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="164" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3a/JFKBerlinSpeech.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="300" data-file-height="224" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy delivering his speech in <a href="/wiki/West_Berlin" title="West Berlin">West Berlin</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1963, Germany was enduring a time of particular vulnerability due to Soviet aggression to the east as well as the impending retirement of West German Chancellor <a href="/wiki/Adenauer" class="mw-redirect" title="Adenauer">Adenauer</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993534_248-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993534-248">&#91;247&#93;</a></sup> At the same time, French President Charles de Gaulle was trying to build a Franco-West German counterweight to the American and Soviet spheres of influence.<sup id="cite_ref-249" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-249">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-250" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-250">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-251" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-251">&#91;250&#93;</a></sup> To Kennedy's eyes, this Franco-German cooperation seemed directed against <a href="/wiki/NATO" title="NATO">NATO</a>'s influence in Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-252" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-252">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To reinforce the U.S. alliance with West Germany, Kennedy travelled to West Germany and West Berlin in June 1963. On June 26, Kennedy toured West Berlin, culminating in a public speech at <a href="/wiki/West_Berlin" title="West Berlin">West Berlin</a>'s city hall in front of hundreds of thousands of enthusiastic Berliners.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDaum2008125–63_253-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaum2008125–63-253">&#91;252&#93;</a></sup>  He reiterated the American commitment to Germany and criticized communism and was met with an ecstatic response from the massive audience.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDallek2003624_254-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek2003624-254">&#91;253&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy used the construction of the Berlin Wall as an example of the failures of communism: "Freedom has many difficulties, and democracy is not perfect. But we have never had to put a wall up to keep our people in, to prevent them from leaving us." The speech is known for its famous phrase <i>"<a href="/wiki/Ich_bin_ein_Berliner" title="Ich bin ein Berliner">Ich bin ein Berliner</a>"</i> ("I am a Berliner"), which Kennedy himself had begun to try out in preparation for the trip.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDaum2008147–56_255-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaum2008147–56-255">&#91;254&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy remarked to Ted Sorensen afterwards: "We'll never have another day like this one, as long as we live."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993537_256-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993537-256">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Israel">Israel</span></h4>
<p>In 1960, Kennedy stated, "Israel will endure and flourish. It is the child of hope and the home of the brave. It can neither be broken by adversity nor demoralized by success. It carries the shield of democracy and it honors the sword of freedom."<sup id="cite_ref-257" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-257">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As president, Kennedy initiated the creation of security ties with Israel, and he is credited as the founder of the US-Israeli military alliance, which would be continued under subsequent presidents. Kennedy ended the arms embargo that the Eisenhower and Truman administrations had enforced on Israel. Describing the protection of Israel as a moral and national commitment, he was the first to introduce the concept of a "special relationship" (as he described it to <a href="/wiki/Golda_Meir" title="Golda Meir">Golda Meir</a>) between the U.S. and Israel.<sup id="cite_ref-258" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-258">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kennedy-Golda_Meir.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Kennedy-Golda_Meir.jpg/170px-Kennedy-Golda_Meir.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="258" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Kennedy-Golda_Meir.jpg/255px-Kennedy-Golda_Meir.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Kennedy-Golda_Meir.jpg/340px-Kennedy-Golda_Meir.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="1824" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy with Israeli Foreign Minister <a href="/wiki/Golda_Meir" title="Golda Meir">Golda Meir</a>, December 27, 1962</figcaption></figure>
<p>Kennedy extended the first informal security guarantees to Israel in 1962 and, beginning in 1963, was the first U.S. president to allow the sale to Israel of advanced U.S. weaponry (the <a href="/wiki/MIM-23_Hawk" title="MIM-23 Hawk">MIM-23 Hawk</a>) as well as to provide diplomatic support for Israeli policies, which were opposed by Arab neighbors; those policies included Israel's water project on the <a href="/wiki/Jordan_River" title="Jordan River">Jordan River</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-259" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-259">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As a result of this newly created security alliance, Kennedy also encountered tensions with the Israeli government over the production of nuclear materials in <a href="/wiki/Dimona" title="Dimona">Dimona</a>, which he believed could instigate a nuclear arms-race in the Middle East. After the existence of a nuclear plant was initially denied by the Israeli government, <a href="/wiki/David_Ben-Gurion" title="David Ben-Gurion">David Ben-Gurion</a> stated in a speech to the Israeli <a href="/wiki/Knesset" title="Knesset">Knesset</a> on December 21, 1960, that the purpose of the nuclear plant at <a href="/wiki/Beersheba" title="Beersheba">Beersheba</a> was for "research in problems of arid zones and desert flora and fauna".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalt2008201_260-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalt2008201-260">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup> When Ben-Gurion met with Kennedy in New York, he claimed that Dimona was being developed to provide nuclear power for desalinization and other peaceful purposes "for the time being".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalt2008201_260-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalt2008201-260">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1963 the Kennedy administration was engaged in a now-declassified diplomatic standoff with the leaders of Israel.<sup id="cite_ref-Haaretz2019_261-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Haaretz2019-261">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-262" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-262">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup> In a May 1963 letter to Ben-Gurion, Kennedy wrote that he was skeptical and stated that American support to Israel could be in jeopardy if reliable information on the Israeli nuclear program was not forthcoming, Ben-Gurion repeated previous reassurances that Dimona was being developed for peaceful purposes. The Israeli government resisted American pressure to open its nuclear facilities to <a href="/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency" title="International Atomic Energy Agency">International Atomic Energy Agency</a> (IAEA) inspections. In 1962 the U.S. and Israeli governments had agreed to an annual inspection regime. A science attaché at the embassy in Tel Aviv concluded that parts of the Dimona facility had been shut down temporarily to mislead American scientists when they visited.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalt2008202_263-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalt2008202-263">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>According to <a href="/wiki/Seymour_Hersh" title="Seymour Hersh">Seymour Hersh</a>, the Israelis set up false control rooms to show the Americans. Israeli lobbyist Abe Feinberg stated: "It was part of my job to tip them off that Kennedy was insisting on [an inspection]."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalt2008202_263-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalt2008202-263">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> Hersh contends that the inspections were conducted in such a way that it "guaranteed that the whole procedure would be little more than a whitewash, as the president and his senior advisors had to understand: the American inspection team would have to schedule its visits well in advance, and with the full acquiescence of Israel."<sup id="cite_ref-264" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-264">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Marc_Trachtenberg" title="Marc Trachtenberg">Marc Trachtenberg</a> argued that "[a]lthough [he was] well aware of what the Israelis were doing, Kennedy chose to take this as satisfactory evidence of Israeli compliance with America's non-proliferation policy."<sup id="cite_ref-265" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-265">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup> The documents reveal the deep concern the Kennedy Administration had over Dimona, and while Kennedy understood the United States and the international community may not be capable of preventing Israel or any nation, he certainly was not satisfied to learn Israel was using Dimona for the production of plutonium.<sup id="cite_ref-266" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-266">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup> The American who led the inspection team stated that the essential goal of the inspections was to find "ways to not reach the point of taking action against Israel's nuclear weapons program".<sup id="cite_ref-267" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-267">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Rodger_Davies" title="Rodger Davies">Rodger Davies</a>, the director of the State Department's Office of Near Eastern Affairs, concluded in March 1965 that Israel was developing <a href="/wiki/Nuclear_weapons" class="mw-redirect" title="Nuclear weapons">nuclear weapons</a>. He reported that Israel's target date for achieving nuclear capability was 1968–1969.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalt2008203_268-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalt2008203-268">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup> On May 1, 1968, Undersecretary of State <a href="/wiki/Nicholas_Katzenbach" title="Nicholas Katzenbach">Nicholas Katzenbach</a> told President Johnson that Dimona was producing enough plutonium to produce two bombs a year. The State Department argued that if Israel wanted arms, it should accept international supervision of its nuclear program.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalt2008202_263-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalt2008202-263">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> Dimona was never placed under IAEA safeguards. Attempts to write Israeli adherence to the <a href="/wiki/Nuclear_Non-Proliferation_Treaty" class="mw-redirect" title="Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty">Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty</a> (NPT) into contracts for the supply of U.S. weapons continued throughout 1968.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalt2008201–205_269-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalt2008201–205-269">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Israeli national interests to an extent were also at odds with Kennedy's endorsement of the United Nation's Johnson Plan, which devised a plan to return a small percentage of displaced Palestinians from the war of 1948 into what was by then, Israel. This continuation of the late UN Secretary General <a href="/wiki/Dag_Hammarskjold" class="mw-redirect" title="Dag Hammarskjold">Dag Hammarskjold</a>'s plan for Palestinian repatriation particularity disturbed persons who had a hard-line view of even Arab resettlement in Israel, or the more heavily feared, full repatriation. The Johnson plan was spearheaded by the Palestine Conciliation Commission's Joseph Ersey Johnson, while the United Nations attempted to oversee progression from writing - into action.<sup id="cite_ref-270" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-270">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-271" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-271">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Iraq">Iraq</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_John_F._Kennedy_administration#Iraq" title="Foreign policy of the John F. Kennedy administration">Foreign policy of the John F. Kennedy administration §&#160;Iraq</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kennedy_with_Shah_of_Iran,_1961.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Kennedy_with_Shah_of_Iran%2C_1961.jpg/220px-Kennedy_with_Shah_of_Iran%2C_1961.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="218" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Kennedy_with_Shah_of_Iran%2C_1961.jpg/330px-Kennedy_with_Shah_of_Iran%2C_1961.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Kennedy_with_Shah_of_Iran%2C_1961.jpg/440px-Kennedy_with_Shah_of_Iran%2C_1961.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1000" data-file-height="991" /></a><figcaption>Shah <a href="/wiki/Mohammad_Reza_Pahlavi" title="Mohammad Reza Pahlavi">Mohammad Reza Pahlavi</a> of Iran, Kennedy, and U.S. Defense Secretary <a href="/wiki/Robert_McNamara" title="Robert McNamara">Robert McNamara</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Cabinet_Room_(White_House)" title="Cabinet Room (White House)">White House Cabinet Room</a> on April 13, 1962</figcaption></figure>
<p>Relations between the United States and Iraq became strained following the overthrow of the Iraqi monarchy on July 14, 1958, which resulted in the declaration of a republican government led by Brigadier <a href="/wiki/Abd_al-Karim_Qasim" title="Abd al-Karim Qasim">Abd al-Karim Qasim</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGibson20153–5_272-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGibson20153–5-272">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup> On June 25, 1961, Qasim mobilized troops along the border between Iraq and <a href="/wiki/Kuwait" title="Kuwait">Kuwait</a>, declaring the latter nation "an indivisible part of Iraq" and causing a short-lived "Kuwait Crisis". The United Kingdom—which had just granted Kuwait independence on June 19, and whose economy was dependent on Kuwaiti oil—responded on July 1 by dispatching 5,000 troops to the country to deter an Iraqi invasion. At the same time, Kennedy dispatched a U.S. Navy task force to <a href="/wiki/Bahrain" title="Bahrain">Bahrain</a>, and the UK, at the urging of the Kennedy administration, brought the dispute to United Nations Security Council, where the proposed resolution was vetoed by the Soviet Union. The situation was resolved in October, when the British troops were withdrawn and replaced by a 4,000-strong <a href="/wiki/Arab_League" title="Arab League">Arab League</a> force, which acted as a barrier against the Iraqi threat.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGibson201536_273-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGibson201536-273">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In December 1961, Qasim's government passed Public Law 80, which restricted the partially American-controlled <a href="/wiki/Iraq_Petroleum_Company" title="Iraq Petroleum Company">Iraq Petroleum Company</a> (IPC)'s <a href="/wiki/Concessionary_holding" class="mw-redirect" title="Concessionary holding">concessionary holding</a> to those areas in which oil was actually being produced, effectively expropriating 99.5% of the IPC concession. U.S. officials were alarmed by the expropriation as well as the recent Soviet veto of an Egyptian-sponsored UN resolution requesting the admittance of Kuwait as UN member state, which they believed were connected. Senior National Security Council adviser <a href="/wiki/Robert_Komer" title="Robert Komer">Robert Komer</a> worried that if the IPC ceased production in response, Qasim might "grab Kuwait" (thus achieving a "stranglehold" on Middle Eastern oil production) or "throw himself into Russian arms". Komer also made note of widespread rumors that a nationalist coup against Qasim could be imminent, and had the potential to "get Iraq back on [a] more neutral keel".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGibson201537,_40–42_274-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGibson201537,_40–42-274">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In April 1962, the State Department issued new guidelines on Iraq that were intended to increase American influence there. Meanwhile, Kennedy instructed the CIA—under the direction of <a href="/wiki/Archibald_Bulloch_Roosevelt_Jr." title="Archibald Bulloch Roosevelt Jr.">Archibald Bulloch Roosevelt Jr.</a>—to begin making preparations for a military coup against Qasim.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGibson201543–45_275-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGibson201543–45-275">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The anti-imperialist and anti-communist <a href="/wiki/Iraqi_Ba%27ath_Party" class="mw-redirect" title="Iraqi Ba&#39;ath Party">Iraqi Ba'ath Party</a> <a href="/wiki/Ramadan_Revolution" title="Ramadan Revolution">overthrew and executed Qasim in a violent coup</a> on February 8, 1963. While there have been persistent rumors that the CIA orchestrated the coup, declassified documents and the testimony of former CIA officers indicate that there was no direct American involvement, although the CIA was actively seeking a suitable replacement for Qasim within the Iraqi military and had been informed of an earlier Ba'athist coup plot.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGibson201545,_57–58_276-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGibson201545,_57–58-276">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup> The Kennedy administration was pleased with the outcome and ultimately approved a $55-million arms deal for Iraq.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGibson201560–61,_80_277-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGibson201560–61,_80-277">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Ireland">Ireland</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President%27s_Trip_to_Europe-_Motorcade_in_Dublin._President_Kennedy,_motorcade,_spectators._Dublin,_Ireland_-_NARA_-_194227.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/President%27s_Trip_to_Europe-_Motorcade_in_Dublin._President_Kennedy%2C_motorcade%2C_spectators._Dublin%2C_Ireland_-_NARA_-_194227.jpg/220px-President%27s_Trip_to_Europe-_Motorcade_in_Dublin._President_Kennedy%2C_motorcade%2C_spectators._Dublin%2C_Ireland_-_NARA_-_194227.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/President%27s_Trip_to_Europe-_Motorcade_in_Dublin._President_Kennedy%2C_motorcade%2C_spectators._Dublin%2C_Ireland_-_NARA_-_194227.jpg/330px-President%27s_Trip_to_Europe-_Motorcade_in_Dublin._President_Kennedy%2C_motorcade%2C_spectators._Dublin%2C_Ireland_-_NARA_-_194227.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/President%27s_Trip_to_Europe-_Motorcade_in_Dublin._President_Kennedy%2C_motorcade%2C_spectators._Dublin%2C_Ireland_-_NARA_-_194227.jpg/440px-President%27s_Trip_to_Europe-_Motorcade_in_Dublin._President_Kennedy%2C_motorcade%2C_spectators._Dublin%2C_Ireland_-_NARA_-_194227.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2963" data-file-height="2015" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy's motorcade through <a href="/wiki/Cork_(city)" title="Cork (city)">Cork</a>, Ireland on June 28, 1963</figcaption></figure>
<p>During his four-day visit to his ancestral home of Ireland beginning on June 26, 1963,<sup id="cite_ref-278" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-278">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy accepted a grant of <a href="/wiki/Achievement_(heraldry)" title="Achievement (heraldry)">armorial bearings</a> from the <a href="/wiki/Chief_Herald_of_Ireland" class="mw-redirect" title="Chief Herald of Ireland">Chief Herald of Ireland</a>, received honorary degrees from the <a href="/wiki/National_University_of_Ireland" title="National University of Ireland">National University of Ireland</a> and <a href="/wiki/Trinity_College_Dublin" title="Trinity College Dublin">Trinity College Dublin</a>, attended a State Dinner in Dublin, and was conferred with the freedom of the towns and cities of Wexford, Cork, Dublin, Galway, and Limerick.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESorensen1966656_279-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESorensen1966656-279">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-homecoming_280-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-homecoming-280">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup> He visited the cottage at Dunganstown, near <a href="/wiki/New_Ross" title="New Ross">New Ross</a>, County Wexford, where his ancestors had lived before emigrating to America.<sup id="cite_ref-BBC_1963_281-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC_1963-281">&#91;280&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Kennedy also was the first foreign leader to address the <a href="/wiki/Oireachtas" title="Oireachtas">Houses of the Oireachtas</a>, the Irish parliament.<sup id="cite_ref-homecoming_280-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-homecoming-280">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-282" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-282">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-283" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-283">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy later told aides that the trip was the best four days of his life.<sup id="cite_ref-284" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-284">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty">Nuclear Test Ban Treaty</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Partial_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty" title="Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty">Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Kennedy_signs_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty,_07_October_1963.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/President_Kennedy_signs_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty%2C_07_October_1963.jpg/220px-President_Kennedy_signs_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty%2C_07_October_1963.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="201" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/President_Kennedy_signs_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty%2C_07_October_1963.jpg/330px-President_Kennedy_signs_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty%2C_07_October_1963.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/President_Kennedy_signs_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty%2C_07_October_1963.jpg/440px-President_Kennedy_signs_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty%2C_07_October_1963.jpg 2x" data-file-width="760" data-file-height="694" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy signs the <a href="/wiki/Partial_Test_Ban_Treaty" class="mw-redirect" title="Partial Test Ban Treaty">Partial Test Ban Treaty</a>, a major milestone in early <a href="/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament" title="Nuclear disarmament">nuclear disarmament</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Troubled by the long-term dangers of <a href="/wiki/Radioactive_contamination" title="Radioactive contamination">radioactive contamination</a> and <a href="/wiki/Nuclear_proliferation" title="Nuclear proliferation">nuclear weapons proliferation</a>, Kennedy and Khrushchev agreed to negotiate a nuclear test ban treaty, originally conceived in Adlai Stevenson's 1956 presidential campaign.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993552_285-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993552-285">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup> In their Vienna summit meeting in June 1961, Khrushchev and Kennedy both reached an informal understanding against nuclear testing, but the Soviet Union began testing nuclear weapons that September. In response, the United States conducted tests five days later.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993227_286-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993227-286">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup> Shortly afterwards, new U.S. satellites began delivering images that made it clear that the Soviets were substantially behind the U.S. in the arms race.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993229_287-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993229-287">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup> Nevertheless, the greater nuclear strength of the U.S. was of little value as long as the U.S.S.R. perceived itself to be at parity.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993243_288-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993243-288">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In July 1963, Kennedy sent <a href="/wiki/W._Averell_Harriman" title="W. Averell Harriman">W. Averell Harriman</a> to Moscow to negotiate a treaty with the Soviets.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993542_289-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993542-289">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup> The introductory sessions included Khrushchev, who later delegated Soviet representation to <a href="/wiki/Andrei_Gromyko" title="Andrei Gromyko">Andrei Gromyko</a>. It quickly became clear that a comprehensive test ban would not be implemented, due largely to the reluctance of the Soviets to allow inspections that would verify compliance.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993548_290-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993548-290">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ultimately, the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union were the initial signatories to a limited treaty, which prohibited atomic testing on the ground, in the atmosphere, or underwater, but not underground. The U.S. Senate ratified this, and Kennedy signed it into law in October 1963. France was quick to declare that it was free to continue developing and testing its nuclear defenses.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993550_291-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993550-291">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Peace_Corps">Peace Corps</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1134653256"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096940132"><div class="side-box side-box-right listen noprint"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1126788409">
<div class="side-box-flex">
<div class="side-box-image"><figure class="mw-halign-center" typeof="mw:File"><span><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/50px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png" decoding="async" width="50" height="50" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/75px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/100px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="160" data-file-height="160" /></span><figcaption></figcaption></figure></div>
<div class="side-box-text plainlist"><div class="haudio">
<div class="listen-file-header"><a href="/wiki/File:JFK_Establishment_of_the_Peace_Corps_edit.ogg" title="File:JFK Establishment of the Peace Corps edit.ogg">Establishment of the Peace Corps</a></div>
<div><span typeof="mw:File"><span><audio id="mwe_player_6" controls="" preload="none" class="mw-file-element" width="232" style="width:232px;" data-durationhint="83" data-mwtitle="JFK_Establishment_of_the_Peace_Corps_edit.ogg" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/56/JFK_Establishment_of_the_Peace_Corps_edit.ogg" type="audio/ogg; codecs=&quot;vorbis&quot;" data-title="Original Ogg file (71 kbps)" data-shorttitle="Ogg source" data-width="0" data-height="0" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/5/56/JFK_Establishment_of_the_Peace_Corps_edit.ogg/JFK_Establishment_of_the_Peace_Corps_edit.ogg.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" data-title="MP3" data-shorttitle="MP3" data-transcodekey="mp3" data-width="0" data-height="0" /></audio></span></span></div>
<div class="description">John F. Kennedy's announcement</div></div></div></div>
<div class="side-box-abovebelow"><hr /><i class="selfreference">Problems playing this file? See <a href="/wiki/Help:Media" title="Help:Media">media help</a>.</i></div>
</div>
<p>In one of his first presidential acts, Kennedy asked Congress to create the <a href="/wiki/Peace_Corps" title="Peace Corps">Peace Corps</a>. His brother-in-law, <a href="/wiki/Sargent_Shriver" title="Sargent Shriver">Sargent Shriver</a>, was its first director.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDallek2003338–339_292-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek2003338–339-292">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup> Through this program, Americans volunteered to help developing nations in fields like education, farming, health care, and construction. The organization grew to 5,000 members by March 1963 and 10,000 the year after.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESchlesinger2002606–607_293-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger2002606–607-293">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup> Since 1961, over 200,000 Americans have joined the Peace Corps, representing 139 countries.<sup id="cite_ref-294" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-294">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-295" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-295">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Domestic_policy">Domestic policy</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/New_Frontier" title="New Frontier">New Frontier</a></div>
<p>Kennedy called his domestic program the "New Frontier". It ambitiously promised federal funding for education, medical care for the elderly, economic aid to rural regions, and government intervention to halt the recession. He also promised an end to <a href="/wiki/Racial_discrimination" title="Racial discrimination">racial discrimination</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-Jaikumar_2011_296-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Jaikumar_2011-296">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup> although his agenda, which included the endorsement of the <a href="/wiki/Voter_Education_Project" title="Voter Education Project">Voter Education Project</a> (VEP) in 1962, produced little progress in areas such as Mississippi, where the "VEP concluded that discrimination was so entrenched".<sup id="cite_ref-297" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-297">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-298" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-298">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In his 1963 <a href="/wiki/State_of_the_Union_address" class="mw-redirect" title="State of the Union address">State of the Union address</a>, he proposed substantial tax reform and a reduction in income tax rates from the current range of 20–90% to a range of 14–65% as well as a reduction in the corporate tax rates from 52 to 47%. Kennedy added that the top rate should be set at 70% if certain deductions were not eliminated for high-income earners.<sup id="cite_ref-Jaikumar_2011_296-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Jaikumar_2011-296">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup> Congress did not act until 1964, a year after his death, when the top individual rate was lowered to 70%, and the top corporate rate was set at 48%.<sup id="cite_ref-299" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-299">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To the <a href="/wiki/Economic_Club_of_New_York" title="Economic Club of New York">Economic Club of New York</a>, he spoke in 1963 of "...&#160;the paradoxical truth that tax rates are too high and revenues too low; and the soundest way to raise revenue in the long term is to lower rates now."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993453_300-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993453-300">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup> Congress passed few of Kennedy's major programs during his lifetime but did vote them through in 1964 and 1965 under his successor Johnson.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBarnes20078_301-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes20078-301">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Economy">Economy</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Recession_of_1960%E2%80%931961" title="Recession of 1960–1961">Recession of 1960–1961</a> and <a href="/wiki/Kennedy_Slide_of_1962" title="Kennedy Slide of 1962">Kennedy Slide of 1962</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Bill_Signing-_Manpower_Development_and_Training_Act_of_1962._President_Kennedy,_Secretary_of_Labor_Arthur_Goldberg..._-_NARA_-_194205.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Bill_Signing-_Manpower_Development_and_Training_Act_of_1962._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_of_Labor_Arthur_Goldberg..._-_NARA_-_194205.jpg/200px-Bill_Signing-_Manpower_Development_and_Training_Act_of_1962._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_of_Labor_Arthur_Goldberg..._-_NARA_-_194205.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="200" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Bill_Signing-_Manpower_Development_and_Training_Act_of_1962._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_of_Labor_Arthur_Goldberg..._-_NARA_-_194205.jpg/300px-Bill_Signing-_Manpower_Development_and_Training_Act_of_1962._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_of_Labor_Arthur_Goldberg..._-_NARA_-_194205.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Bill_Signing-_Manpower_Development_and_Training_Act_of_1962._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_of_Labor_Arthur_Goldberg..._-_NARA_-_194205.jpg/400px-Bill_Signing-_Manpower_Development_and_Training_Act_of_1962._President_Kennedy%2C_Secretary_of_Labor_Arthur_Goldberg..._-_NARA_-_194205.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2700" data-file-height="2700" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy signing the <a href="/wiki/New_Frontier#Unemployment" title="New Frontier">Manpower Development and Training Act</a>, March 1962</figcaption></figure>
<p>Kennedy ended a period of tight fiscal policies, loosening monetary policy to keep <a href="/wiki/Interest_rate" title="Interest rate">interest rates</a> down and to encourage growth of the economy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFrum2000293_302-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrum2000293-302">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup> He presided over the first government budget to top the $100&#160;billion mark, in 1962, and his first budget in 1961 resulted in the nation's first non-war, non-recession <a href="/wiki/Government_budget_deficit" class="mw-redirect" title="Government budget deficit">deficit</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFrum2000324_303-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrum2000324-303">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup> The economy, which had been through two recessions in three years and was in one when Kennedy took office, accelerated notably throughout his administration. Despite low inflation and interest rates, the GDP had grown by an average of only 2.2% per annum during the Eisenhower administration (scarcely more than population growth at the time), and it had declined by 1% during Eisenhower's last twelve months in office.<sup id="cite_ref-Bureau_of_Economic_Analysis_304-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bureau_of_Economic_Analysis-304">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The economy turned around and prospered during Kennedy's years as president. The GDP expanded by an average of 5.5% from early-1961 to late-1963,<sup id="cite_ref-Bureau_of_Economic_Analysis_304-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bureau_of_Economic_Analysis-304">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup> while inflation remained steady at around 1% and unemployment eased.<sup id="cite_ref-GDP_1913_to_2002_305-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-GDP_1913_to_2002-305">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup> Industrial production rose by 15% and motor vehicle sales increased by 40%.<sup id="cite_ref-Statistical_Abstract_1964_306-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Statistical_Abstract_1964-306">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup> This rate of growth in GDP and industry continued until 1969 and has yet to be repeated for such a sustained period of time.<sup id="cite_ref-Bureau_of_Economic_Analysis_304-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bureau_of_Economic_Analysis-304">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Attorney General Robert Kennedy took the position that <a href="/wiki/Roger_Blough" title="Roger Blough">steel executives</a> had illegally colluded to fix prices. He stated, "We're going for broke. [...] their expense accounts, where they've been and what they've been doing. [...] the FBI is to interview them all. [...] we can't lose this."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993298_307-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993298-307">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup> The administration's actions influenced <a href="/wiki/U.S._Steel" title="U.S. Steel">U.S. Steel</a> to rescind the price increase.<sup id="cite_ref-Time_1962_308-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Time_1962-308">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal" title="The Wall Street Journal">The Wall Street Journal</a></i> wrote that the administration had acted "by naked power, by threats, [and] by agents of the state security police".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEO&#39;Brien2005645_309-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO&#39;Brien2005645-309">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> Yale law professor <a href="/wiki/Charles_Reich" class="mw-redirect" title="Charles Reich">Charles Reich</a> opined in <i><a href="/wiki/The_New_Republic" title="The New Republic">The New Republic</a></i> that the administration had violated civil liberties by calling a grand jury to indict U.S. Steel for collusion so quickly.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEO&#39;Brien2005645_309-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO&#39;Brien2005645-309">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> An editorial in <i><a href="/wiki/The_New_York_Times" title="The New York Times">The New York Times</a></i> praised Kennedy's actions and said that the steel industry's price increase "imperil[ed] the economic welfare of the country by inviting a tidal wave of inflation".<sup id="cite_ref-NY_Times_1962_310-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NY_Times_1962-310">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup> Nevertheless, the administration's Bureau of Budget reported the price increase would have caused a net gain for the GDP as well as a net budget surplus.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993300_311-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993300-311">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup> The stock market, which had steadily declined since Kennedy's election in 1960, dropped 10% shortly after the administration's action on the steel industry took place.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993318–320_312-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993318–320-312">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Federal_and_military_death_penalty">Federal and military death penalty</span></h4>
<p>During his administration, Kennedy oversaw the last federal execution prior to <i><a href="/wiki/Furman_v._Georgia" title="Furman v. Georgia">Furman v. Georgia</a></i>, a 1972 case that led to a moratorium on federal executions.<sup id="cite_ref-313" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-313">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Victor_Feguer" title="Victor Feguer">Victor Feguer</a> was sentenced to death by an Iowa federal court and was executed on March 15, 1963.<sup id="cite_ref-Goldberg_2001_314-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Goldberg_2001-314">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy commuted a death sentence imposed by a military court on seaman Jimmie Henderson on February 12, 1962, changing the penalty to life in prison.<sup id="cite_ref-Riechmann_2008_315-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Riechmann_2008-315">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On March 22, 1962, Kennedy signed into law HR5143 (PL87-423), which abolished the mandatory death penalty for <a href="/wiki/First_degree_murder_in_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="First degree murder in the United States">first degree murder</a> suspects in the District of Columbia, the only remaining jurisdiction in the United States with such a penalty.<sup id="cite_ref-JFKlibrary.org_leg_316-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-JFKlibrary.org_leg-316">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup> The death penalty has not been applied in the District of Columbia since 1957 and has now been abolished.<sup id="cite_ref-317" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-317">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Civil_rights_movement">Civil rights movement</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Civil_rights_movement" title="Civil rights movement">Civil rights movement</a></div>
<p>The turbulent end of state-sanctioned racial discrimination was one of the most pressing domestic issues of the 1960s. "<a href="/wiki/Jim_Crow" class="mw-redirect" title="Jim Crow">Jim Crow</a>" <a href="/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States" title="Racial segregation in the United States">segregation</a> was the established law in the <a href="/wiki/Deep_South" title="Deep South">Deep South</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Grantham_p156_318-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Grantham_p156-318">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/U.S._Supreme_Court" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Supreme Court">U.S. Supreme Court</a> had ruled in 1954 in <i><a href="/wiki/Brown_v._Board_of_Education" title="Brown v. Board of Education">Brown v. Board of Education</a></i> that <a href="/wiki/Racial_segregation" title="Racial segregation">racial segregation</a> in public schools was unconstitutional. Many schools, especially those in southern states, did not obey the Supreme Court's decision. The Court also prohibited segregation at other public facilities (such as buses, restaurants, theaters, courtrooms, bathrooms, and beaches) but it continued nonetheless.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDallek2003292–293_319-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek2003292–293-319">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Thurgood_Marshall_1957-09-17.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Thurgood_Marshall_1957-09-17.jpg/170px-Thurgood_Marshall_1957-09-17.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="256" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Thurgood_Marshall_1957-09-17.jpg/255px-Thurgood_Marshall_1957-09-17.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Thurgood_Marshall_1957-09-17.jpg/340px-Thurgood_Marshall_1957-09-17.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3344" data-file-height="5040" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Thurgood_Marshall" title="Thurgood Marshall">Thurgood Marshall</a>, appointed to the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit by Kennedy in May 1961</figcaption></figure>
<p>Kennedy verbally supported <a href="/wiki/Racial_integration" title="Racial integration">racial integration</a> and <a href="/wiki/Civil_rights" class="mw-redirect" title="Civil rights">civil rights</a>; during his 1960 presidential campaign, he telephoned <a href="/wiki/Coretta_Scott_King" title="Coretta Scott King">Coretta Scott King</a>, wife of the Reverend <a href="/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr." title="Martin Luther King Jr.">Martin Luther King Jr.</a>, who had been jailed while trying to integrate a department store lunch counter.
