Robert Kennedy called Georgia governor <a href="/wiki/Ernest_Vandiver" title="Ernest Vandiver">Ernest Vandiver</a> and obtained King's release from prison, which drew additional black support to his brother's candidacy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDallek2003292–293_319-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek2003292–293-319">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup> Upon taking office in 1961, Kennedy postponed promised civil rights legislation he made while campaigning in 1960, recognizing that conservative Southern Democrats controlled congressional legislation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002487_320-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002487-320">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup> During his first year in office, Kennedy appointed many Black people to office including his May appointment of civil rights attorney <a href="/wiki/Thurgood_Marshall" title="Thurgood Marshall">Thurgood Marshall</a> to the federal bench.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490_321-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490-321">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In his first State of the Union Address in January 1961, President Kennedy said, "The denial of constitutional rights to some of our fellow Americans on account of race—at the ballot box and elsewhere—disturbs the national conscience, and subjects us to the charge of world opinion that our democracy is not equal to the high promise of our heritage."<sup id="cite_ref-322" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-322">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy believed the grassroots movement for civil rights would anger many Southern whites and make it more difficult to pass civil rights laws in Congress, including anti-poverty legislation, and he distanced himself from it.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBryant200660,_66_323-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryant200660,_66-323">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Kennedy was concerned with other issues in the early part of his administration, such as the Cold War, Bay of Pigs fiasco, and the situation in Southeast Asia. As articulated by his brother Robert, the administration's early priority was to "keep the president out of this civil rights mess". Civil rights movement participants, mainly those on the front line in the South, viewed Kennedy as lukewarm,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490_321-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490-321">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup> especially concerning the <a href="/wiki/Freedom_Riders" title="Freedom Riders">Freedom Riders</a>, who organized an integrated public transportation effort in the south, and who were repeatedly met with white mob violence, including by law enforcement officers, both federal and state. Kennedy assigned <a href="/wiki/Federal_marshal" class="mw-redirect" title="Federal marshal">federal marshals</a> to protect the Freedom Riders rather than using federal troops or uncooperative FBI agents.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490_321-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490-321">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup> Robert Kennedy, speaking for the president, urged the Freedom Riders to "get off the buses and leave the matter to peaceful settlement in the courts".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993123–126_324-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993123–126-324">&#91;323&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy feared sending federal troops would stir up "hated memories of <a href="/wiki/Reconstruction_Era" class="mw-redirect" title="Reconstruction Era">Reconstruction</a>" after the <a href="/wiki/American_Civil_War" title="American Civil War">Civil War</a> among conservative Southern whites.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490_321-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490-321">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On March 6, 1961, Kennedy signed <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_10925" title="Executive Order 10925">Executive Order 10925</a>, which required government contractors to "take affirmative action to ensure that applicants are employed and that employees are treated during employment without regard to their race, creed, color, or national origin".<sup id="cite_ref-325" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-325">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup> It established the <a href="/wiki/Equal_Employment_Opportunity_Commission#Background" title="Equal Employment Opportunity Commission">President's Committee on Equal Employment Opportunity</a>. Displeased with Kennedy's pace addressing the issue of segregation, Martin Luther King Jr. and his associates produced a document in 1962 calling on Kennedy to follow in the footsteps of <a href="/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln" title="Abraham Lincoln">Abraham Lincoln</a> and use an Executive Order to deliver a blow for civil rights as a kind of <a href="/wiki/Second_Emancipation_Proclamation" title="Second Emancipation Proclamation">Second Emancipation Proclamation</a>. Kennedy did not execute the order.<sup id="cite_ref-kennedyandking1_326-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-kennedyandking1-326">&#91;325&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mary_Collins,_Mayor_John_F._Collins,_President_John_F._Kennedy,_and_unidentified_woman_and_men_(10559425146).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Mary_Collins%2C_Mayor_John_F._Collins%2C_President_John_F._Kennedy%2C_and_unidentified_woman_and_men_%2810559425146%29.jpg/220px-Mary_Collins%2C_Mayor_John_F._Collins%2C_President_John_F._Kennedy%2C_and_unidentified_woman_and_men_%2810559425146%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="217" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Mary_Collins%2C_Mayor_John_F._Collins%2C_President_John_F._Kennedy%2C_and_unidentified_woman_and_men_%2810559425146%29.jpg/330px-Mary_Collins%2C_Mayor_John_F._Collins%2C_President_John_F._Kennedy%2C_and_unidentified_woman_and_men_%2810559425146%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Mary_Collins%2C_Mayor_John_F._Collins%2C_President_John_F._Kennedy%2C_and_unidentified_woman_and_men_%2810559425146%29.jpg/440px-Mary_Collins%2C_Mayor_John_F._Collins%2C_President_John_F._Kennedy%2C_and_unidentified_woman_and_men_%2810559425146%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4708" data-file-height="4646" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy with <a href="/wiki/Mayor_of_Boston" title="Mayor of Boston">Boston Mayor</a> <a href="/wiki/John_F._Collins" title="John F. Collins">John F. Collins</a> (1960–1968) and his wife. On November 20, 1962, Kennedy issued <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_11063" title="Executive Order 11063">Executive Order 11063</a> requiring all federal agencies to prevent racial discrimination in federally funded <a href="/wiki/Subsidized_housing_in_the_United_States" title="Subsidized housing in the United States">subsidized housing in the United States</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In September 1962, <a href="/wiki/James_Meredith" title="James Meredith">James Meredith</a> enrolled at the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Mississippi" title="University of Mississippi">University of Mississippi</a> but was prevented from entering. In response to that, Attorney General Robert Kennedy sent 127 <a href="/wiki/United_States_Marshals_Service" title="United States Marshals Service">U.S. Marshals</a> and 316 <a href="/wiki/United_States_Border_Patrol" title="United States Border Patrol">U.S. Border Patrol</a> and 97 <a href="/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Prisons" title="Federal Bureau of Prisons">Federal correctional officers</a> who were deputized as marshals.<sup id="cite_ref-327" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-327">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Ole_Miss_riot_of_1962" title="Ole Miss riot of 1962">Ole Miss riot of 1962</a> left two civilians dead and 300 people injured, prompting President Kennedy to send in 3,000 troops to quell the riot.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBryant200671_328-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryant200671-328">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup> Meredith did finally enroll for a class, and Kennedy regretted not sending in troops earlier. Kennedy began doubting as to whether the "evils of Reconstruction" of the 1860s and 1870s he had been taught or believed in were true.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490_321-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002490-321">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup> The instigating subculture during the Ole Miss riot, and many other racially ignited events, was the <a href="/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan" title="Ku Klux Klan">Ku Klux Klan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Gitlin_p29_329-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Gitlin_p29-329">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup> On November 20, 1962, Kennedy signed <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_11063" title="Executive Order 11063">Executive Order 11063</a>, which prohibited racial discrimination in federally supported housing or "related facilities".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDallek2003580_330-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek2003580-330">&#91;329&#93;</a></sup> Despite this, in <a href="/wiki/Boston" title="Boston">Boston</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Boston_Housing_Authority" title="Boston Housing Authority">Boston Housing Authority</a> (BHA) Board would continue to actively <a href="/wiki/Housing_segregation_in_the_United_States" title="Housing segregation in the United States">segregate</a> the <a href="/wiki/Subsidized_housing_in_the_United_States" title="Subsidized housing in the United States">public housing developments</a> in the city during the <a href="/wiki/John_F._Collins#Public_housing" title="John F. Collins">John F. Collins administration</a> (1960–1968), with BHA departments engaging in bureaucratic resistance against integration through at least 1966 and the Board retaining control over tenant assignment until 1968.<sup id="cite_ref-Vale_pp._301–320_331-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Vale_pp._301–320-331">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Both Kennedy and Robert Kennedy were concerned about King's ties to suspected communists <a href="/wiki/Jack_O%27Dell" title="Jack O&#39;Dell">Jack O'Dell</a> and <a href="/wiki/Stanley_Levison" title="Stanley Levison">Stanley Levison</a>. After Kennedy and his civil rights expert <a href="/wiki/Harris_Wofford" title="Harris Wofford">Harris Wofford</a> pressed King to ask both men to resign from the SCLC, King agreed to ask only O'Dell to resign from the organization and allowed Levison, whom he regarded as a trusted advisor, to remain.<sup id="cite_ref-kennedyandking2_332-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-kennedyandking2-332">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In early 1963, Kennedy related to Martin Luther King Jr. his thoughts on the prospects for civil rights legislation: "If we get into a long fight over this in Congress, it will bottleneck everything else, and we will still get no bill."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993467_333-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993467-333">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup> Civil rights clashes were on the rise that year.<sup id="cite_ref-334" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-334">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup> His brother Robert and Ted Sorensen pressed Kennedy to take more initiative on the legislative front.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993515_335-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993515-335">&#91;334&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Kennedy_addresses_nation_on_Civil_Rights,_11_June_1963.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/President_Kennedy_addresses_nation_on_Civil_Rights%2C_11_June_1963.jpg/220px-President_Kennedy_addresses_nation_on_Civil_Rights%2C_11_June_1963.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="279" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/President_Kennedy_addresses_nation_on_Civil_Rights%2C_11_June_1963.jpg/330px-President_Kennedy_addresses_nation_on_Civil_Rights%2C_11_June_1963.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/President_Kennedy_addresses_nation_on_Civil_Rights%2C_11_June_1963.jpg/440px-President_Kennedy_addresses_nation_on_Civil_Rights%2C_11_June_1963.jpg 2x" data-file-width="760" data-file-height="963" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy's <a href="/wiki/Report_to_the_American_People_on_Civil_Rights" title="Report to the American People on Civil Rights">Report to the American People on Civil Rights</a>, June 11, 1963</figcaption></figure>
<p>On June 11, 1963, President Kennedy intervened when Alabama Governor <a href="/wiki/George_Wallace" title="George Wallace">George Wallace</a> blocked the <a href="/wiki/Stand_in_the_Schoolhouse_Door" title="Stand in the Schoolhouse Door">doorway</a> to the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Alabama" title="University of Alabama">University of Alabama</a> to stop two African American students, <a href="/wiki/Vivian_Malone" class="mw-redirect" title="Vivian Malone">Vivian Malone</a> and <a href="/wiki/James_Hood" title="James Hood">James Hood</a>, from attending. Wallace moved aside only after being confronted by Deputy Attorney General Nicholas Katzenbach and the Alabama <a href="/wiki/United_States_National_Guard" class="mw-redirect" title="United States National Guard">U.S. National Guard</a>, which had just been federalized by order of the president. That evening Kennedy gave his famous <a href="/wiki/Report_to_the_American_People_on_Civil_Rights" title="Report to the American People on Civil Rights">Report to the American People on Civil Rights</a> on national television and radio, launching his initiative for civil rights legislation—to provide equal access to public schools and other facilities, and greater protection of voting rights.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993521–523_336-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993521–523-336">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-337" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-337">&#91;336&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>His proposals became part of the <a href="/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964" title="Civil Rights Act of 1964">Civil Rights Act of 1964</a>. The day ended with the murder of an NAACP leader, <a href="/wiki/Medgar_Evers" title="Medgar Evers">Medgar Evers</a>, in front of his home in Mississippi.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESchlesinger2002966_338-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger2002966-338">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup> As Kennedy had predicted, the day after his TV speech, and in reaction to it, House Majority leader Carl Albert called to advise him that his two-year signature effort in Congress to combat poverty in Appalachia (Area Redevelopment Administration) had been defeated, primarily by the votes of Southern Democrats and Republicans.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993524_339-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993524-339">&#91;338&#93;</a></sup> When Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr. complimented Kennedy on his remarks, Kennedy bitterly replied, "Yes, and look at what happened to area development the very next day in the House." He then added, "But of course, I had to give that speech, and I'm glad that I did."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECohen2016357_340-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen2016357-340">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup> On June 16, <i><a href="/wiki/The_New_York_Times" title="The New York Times">The New York Times</a></i> published an editorial which argued that while Kennedy had initially "moved too slowly and with little evidence of deep moral commitment" in regards to civil rights he "now demonstrate[d] a genuine sense of urgency about eradicating racial discrimination from our national life".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGoduti2012206_341-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoduti2012206-341">&#91;340&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Earlier, Kennedy had signed the executive order creating the <a href="/wiki/Presidential_Commission_on_the_Status_of_Women" title="Presidential Commission on the Status of Women">Presidential Commission on the Status of Women</a> on December 14, 1961.<sup id="cite_ref-executive_order_342-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-executive_order-342">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup> Former First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt led the commission. The Commission statistics revealed that women were also experiencing discrimination; its final report, documenting legal and cultural barriers, was issued in October 1963.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993433_343-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993433-343">&#91;342&#93;</a></sup> Further, on June 10, 1963, Kennedy signed the <a href="/wiki/Equal_Pay_Act_of_1963" title="Equal Pay Act of 1963">Equal Pay Act of 1963</a>, which amended the <a href="/wiki/Fair_Labor_Standards_Act" class="mw-redirect" title="Fair Labor Standards Act">Fair Labor Standards Act</a> and abolished wage disparity based on sex.<sup id="cite_ref-344" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-344">&#91;343&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Photograph_of_Meeting_with_Leaders_of_the_March_on_Washington_August_28,_1963_-_NARA_-_194276.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Photograph_of_Meeting_with_Leaders_of_the_March_on_Washington_August_28%2C_1963_-_NARA_-_194276.jpg/220px-Photograph_of_Meeting_with_Leaders_of_the_March_on_Washington_August_28%2C_1963_-_NARA_-_194276.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="221" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Photograph_of_Meeting_with_Leaders_of_the_March_on_Washington_August_28%2C_1963_-_NARA_-_194276.jpg/330px-Photograph_of_Meeting_with_Leaders_of_the_March_on_Washington_August_28%2C_1963_-_NARA_-_194276.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Photograph_of_Meeting_with_Leaders_of_the_March_on_Washington_August_28%2C_1963_-_NARA_-_194276.jpg/440px-Photograph_of_Meeting_with_Leaders_of_the_March_on_Washington_August_28%2C_1963_-_NARA_-_194276.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2936" data-file-height="2944" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy meetings with leaders of the <a href="/wiki/March_on_Washington" class="mw-redirect" title="March on Washington">March on Washington</a> in the Oval Office, August 28, 1963</figcaption></figure>
<p>Over a hundred thousand people, predominantly African Americans, gathered in Washington for the civil rights <a href="/wiki/March_on_Washington_for_Jobs_and_Freedom" title="March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom">March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom</a> on August 28, 1963. Kennedy feared the March would have a negative effect on the prospects for the civil rights bills in Congress and declined an invitation to speak. He turned over some of the details of the government's involvement to the Dept. of Justice, which channeled hundreds of thousands of dollars to the six sponsors of the March, including the <a href="/wiki/National_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Colored_People" class="mw-redirect" title="National Association for the Advancement of Colored People">NAACP</a> and Martin Luther King's <a href="/wiki/Southern_Christian_Leadership_Conference" title="Southern Christian Leadership Conference">Southern Christian Leadership Conference</a> (SCLC).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993580–584_345-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993580–584-345">&#91;344&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To ensure a peaceful demonstration, the organizers and Kennedy personally edited speeches that were inflammatory and agreed the March would be held on a Wednesday and would be over at 4:00&#160;pm. Thousands of troops were placed on standby. Kennedy watched King's speech on TV and was very impressed. The March was considered a "triumph of managed protest", and not one arrest relating to the demonstration occurred. Afterwards, the March leaders accepted an invitation to the White House to meet with Kennedy and photos were taken. Kennedy felt that the March was a victory for him as well and bolstered the chances for his civil rights bill.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993580–584_345-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993580–584-345">&#91;344&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Nevertheless, the struggle was far from over. Three weeks later on Sunday, September 15, <a href="/wiki/16th_Street_Baptist_Church_bombing" title="16th Street Baptist Church bombing">a bomb exploded</a> at the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham; by the end of the day, four African American children had died in the explosion, and two other children were shot to death in the aftermath.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993599–600_346-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993599–600-346">&#91;345&#93;</a></sup> Due to this resurgent violence, the civil rights legislation underwent some drastic amendments that critically endangered any prospects for passage of the bill, to the outrage of the president. Kennedy called the congressional leaders to the White House and by the following day the original bill, without the additions, had enough votes to get it out of the House committee.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993628–631_347-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993628–631-347">&#91;346&#93;</a></sup> Gaining Republican support, Senator <a href="/wiki/Everett_Dirksen" title="Everett Dirksen">Everett Dirksen</a> promised the legislation would be brought to a vote preventing a <a href="/wiki/Filibuster_in_the_United_States_Senate" title="Filibuster in the United States Senate">Senate filibuster</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002492_348-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002492-348">&#91;347&#93;</a></sup> The legislation was enacted by Kennedy's successor President Lyndon B. Johnson, prompted by Kennedy's memory, after his assassination in November, enforcing voting rights, public accommodations, employment, education, and the administration of justice.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002492_348-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrauer2002492-348">&#91;347&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Civil_liberties">Civil liberties</span></h4>
<p>In February 1962,<sup id="cite_ref-kingandkennedy3_349-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-kingandkennedy3-349">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup> FBI Director <a href="/wiki/J._Edgar_Hoover" title="J. Edgar Hoover">J. Edgar Hoover</a>, who was suspicious of civil-rights leader <a href="/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr." title="Martin Luther King Jr.">Martin Luther King Jr.</a> and viewed him as an upstart troublemaker,<sup id="cite_ref-american_public_radio_350-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-american_public_radio-350">&#91;349&#93;</a></sup> presented the Kennedy administration with allegations that some of King's close confidants and advisers were communists. Concerned by these allegations, the FBI deployed agents to monitor King in the following months.<sup id="cite_ref-kingandkennedy3_349-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-kingandkennedy3-349">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup> Robert Kennedy and President Kennedy also both warned King to discontinue the suspect associations. After the associations continued, Robert Kennedy issued a written directive authorizing the FBI to wiretap King and other leaders of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, King's civil rights organization, in October 1963.<sup id="cite_ref-kingandkennedy3_349-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-kingandkennedy3-349">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Although Kennedy only gave written approval for limited wiretapping of King's phones "on a trial basis, for a month or so",<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHerst2007372_351-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerst2007372-351">&#91;350&#93;</a></sup> Hoover extended the clearance so his men were "unshackled" to look for evidence in any areas of King's life they deemed worthy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHerst2007372–374_352-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerst2007372–374-352">&#91;351&#93;</a></sup> The wiretapping continued through June 1966 and was revealed in 1968.<sup id="cite_ref-the_atlantic_353-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-the_atlantic-353">&#91;352&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Immigration">Immigration</span></h4>
<p>During the 1960 campaign, Kennedy proposed an overhaul of American immigration and naturalization laws to ban discrimination based on national origin. He saw this proposal as an extension of his planned civil rights agenda as president.<sup id="cite_ref-354" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-354">&#91;353&#93;</a></sup> These reforms later became law through the <a href="/wiki/Immigration_and_Nationality_Act_of_1965" title="Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965">Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965</a>, which dramatically shifted the source of immigration from Northern and Western European countries towards immigration from Latin America and Asia. The policy change also shifted the emphasis on the selection of immigrants in favor of family reunification. The late president's brother, Senator <a href="/wiki/Ted_Kennedy" title="Ted Kennedy">Edward Kennedy</a> of Massachusetts helped steer the legislation through the Senate.<sup id="cite_ref-355" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-355">&#91;354&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Native_American_relations">Native American relations</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Kinzua_Dam#Native_Americans" title="Kinzua Dam">Kinzua Dam §&#160;Native Americans</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Seneca_nation#Kinzua_Dam" class="mw-redirect" title="Seneca nation">Seneca nation §&#160;Kinzua Dam</a></div>
<p>Construction of the <a href="/wiki/Kinzua_Dam" title="Kinzua Dam">Kinzua Dam</a> flooded 10,000 acres (4,000 hectares) of <a href="/wiki/Seneca_nation" class="mw-redirect" title="Seneca nation">Seneca nation</a> land that they had occupied under the <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Canandaigua" title="Treaty of Canandaigua">Treaty of 1794</a>, and forced 600 Seneca to relocate to <a href="/wiki/Salamanca_(town),_New_York" title="Salamanca (town), New York">Salamanca, New York</a>. Kennedy was asked by the <a href="/wiki/American_Civil_Liberties_Union" title="American Civil Liberties Union">American Civil Liberties Union</a> to intervene and to halt the project, but he declined, citing a critical need for flood control. He expressed concern about the plight of the Seneca and directed government agencies to assist in obtaining more land, damages, and assistance to help mitigate their displacement.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBilharz200255_356-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBilharz200255-356">&#91;355&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Kennedy_letter_1961_357-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Kennedy_letter_1961-357">&#91;356&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Space_policy">Space policy</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Space_policy_of_the_United_States" title="Space policy of the United States">Space policy of the United States</a> and <a href="/wiki/Space_Race" title="Space Race">Space Race</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:JFK_inspects_Mercury_capsule,_23_February_1962.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/JFK_inspects_Mercury_capsule%2C_23_February_1962.jpg/220px-JFK_inspects_Mercury_capsule%2C_23_February_1962.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="220" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/JFK_inspects_Mercury_capsule%2C_23_February_1962.jpg/330px-JFK_inspects_Mercury_capsule%2C_23_February_1962.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/JFK_inspects_Mercury_capsule%2C_23_February_1962.jpg/440px-JFK_inspects_Mercury_capsule%2C_23_February_1962.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2674" data-file-height="2673" /></a><figcaption>Accompanied by astronaut <a href="/wiki/John_Glenn" title="John Glenn">John Glenn</a>, Kennedy inspects the Project Mercury capsule <i><a href="/wiki/Friendship_7" class="mw-redirect" title="Friendship 7">Friendship 7</a></i>, February 23, 1962.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Apollo_program" title="Apollo program">Apollo program</a> was conceived early in 1960, during the Eisenhower administration, as a follow-up to <a href="/wiki/Project_Mercury" title="Project Mercury">Project Mercury</a>, to be used as a shuttle to an Earth-orbital <a href="/wiki/Space_station" title="Space station">space station</a>, flights around the Moon, or landing on it. While <a href="/wiki/NASA" title="NASA">NASA</a> went ahead with planning for Apollo, funding for the program was far from certain, given Eisenhower's ambivalent attitude to crewed spaceflight.<sup id="cite_ref-358" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-358">&#91;357&#93;</a></sup> As senator, Kennedy had been opposed to the space program and wanted to terminate it.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993138_359-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993138-359">&#91;358&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kennedy_with_von_Braun.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Kennedy_with_von_Braun.jpg/220px-Kennedy_with_von_Braun.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="178" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Kennedy_with_von_Braun.jpg/330px-Kennedy_with_von_Braun.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Kennedy_with_von_Braun.jpg/440px-Kennedy_with_von_Braun.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2425" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Wernher_von_Braun" title="Wernher von Braun">Wernher von Braun</a> and Kennedy</figcaption></figure>
<p>In constructing his presidential administration, Kennedy elected to retain Eisenhower's last science advisor <a href="/wiki/Jerome_Wiesner" title="Jerome Wiesner">Jerome Wiesner</a> as head of the <a href="/wiki/President%27s_Science_Advisory_Committee" title="President&#39;s Science Advisory Committee">President's Science Advisory Committee</a>. Wiesner was strongly opposed to crewed space exploration,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelson2009145_360-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2009145-360">&#91;359&#93;</a></sup> having issued a report highly critical of Project Mercury.<sup id="cite_ref-361" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-361">&#91;360&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-362" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-362">&#91;361&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy was turned down by seventeen candidates for NASA administrator before the post was accepted by <a href="/wiki/James_E._Webb" title="James E. Webb">James E. Webb</a>, an experienced Washington insider who served President Truman as budget director and undersecretary of state. Webb proved to be adept at obtaining the support of Congress, the President, and the American people.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelson2009146_363-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2009146-363">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy also persuaded Congress to amend the <a href="/wiki/National_Aeronautics_and_Space_Act" title="National Aeronautics and Space Act">National Aeronautics and Space Act</a> to allow him to delegate his chairmanship of the National Aeronautics and Space Council to the Vice President,
<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelson2009146_363-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2009146-363">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKenney2000115–116_364-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKenney2000115–116-364">&#91;363&#93;</a></sup> both because of the knowledge of the space program Johnson gained in the Senate working for <a href="/wiki/The_creation_of_NASA" class="mw-redirect" title="The creation of NASA">the creation of NASA</a>, and to help keep the politically savvy Johnson occupied.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelson2009146_363-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2009146-363">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kennedy_Giving_Historic_Speech_to_Congress_-_GPN-2000-001658.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Kennedy_Giving_Historic_Speech_to_Congress_-_GPN-2000-001658.jpg/220px-Kennedy_Giving_Historic_Speech_to_Congress_-_GPN-2000-001658.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Kennedy_Giving_Historic_Speech_to_Congress_-_GPN-2000-001658.jpg/330px-Kennedy_Giving_Historic_Speech_to_Congress_-_GPN-2000-001658.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Kennedy_Giving_Historic_Speech_to_Congress_-_GPN-2000-001658.jpg/440px-Kennedy_Giving_Historic_Speech_to_Congress_-_GPN-2000-001658.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2940" data-file-height="2230" /></a><figcaption>Kennedy proposing a program to Congress that will land men on the Moon, May 1961. Johnson and Sam Rayburn are seated behind him.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In Kennedy's January 1961 State of the Union address, he suggested international cooperation in space. Khrushchev declined, as the Soviets did not wish to reveal the status of their rocketry and space capabilities.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDallek2003502_365-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek2003502-365">&#91;364&#93;</a></sup> Early in his presidency, Kennedy was poised to dismantle the crewed space program but postponed any decision out of deference to Johnson, who had been a strong supporter of the space program in the Senate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReeves1993138_359-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReeves1993138-359">&#91;358&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>This quickly changed on April 12, 1961, when Soviet cosmonaut <a href="/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin" title="Yuri Gagarin">Yuri Gagarin</a> became the first person to fly in space, reinforcing American fears about being left behind in a technological competition with the Soviet Union.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDallek2003393_366-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek2003393-366">&#91;365&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy now became eager for the U.S. to take the lead in the <a href="/wiki/Space_Race" title="Space Race">Space Race</a>, for reasons of national security and prestige. On April 20, he sent a memo to Johnson, asking him to look into the status of America's space program, and into programs that could offer NASA the opportunity to catch up.<sup id="cite_ref-jfkmemo_367-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-jfkmemo-367">&#91;366&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-368" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-368">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> After consulting with <a href="/wiki/Wernher_von_Braun" title="Wernher von Braun">Wernher von Braun</a>, Johnson responded approximately one week later, concluding that "we are neither making maximum effort nor achieving results necessary if this country is to reach a position of leadership".<sup id="cite_ref-lbjmemo_369-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lbjmemo-369">&#91;368&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-370" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-370">&#91;369&#93;</a></sup> His memo concluded that a crewed Moon landing was far enough in the future that it was likely the United States would achieve it first.<sup id="cite_ref-lbjmemo_369-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lbjmemo-369">&#91;368&#93;</a></sup> Kennedy's advisor Ted Sorensen advised him to support the Moon landing, and on May 25, Kennedy announced the goal in a speech titled "Special Message to the Congress on Urgent National Needs":
</p>
<blockquote><p>... I believe that this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth. No single space project in this period will be more impressive to mankind, or more important for the long-range exploration of space; and none will be so difficult or expensive to accomplish.<sup id="cite_ref-Kennedy_at_Congress_1961_371-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Kennedy_at_Congress_1961-371">&#91;370&#93;</a></sup> <a href="https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Special_Message_to_the_Congress_on_Urgent_National_Needs" class="extiw" title="s:Special Message to the Congress on Urgent National Needs">Full text</a>&#160;<span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/Wikisource" title="Wikisource has information on &quot;Special Message to the Congress on Urgent National Needs&quot;"><img alt="Wikisource has information on &quot;Special Message to the Congress on Urgent National Needs&quot;" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/11px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png" decoding="async" width="11" height="12" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/17px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/22px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="410" data-file-height="430" /></a></span></p></blockquote>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><span><video id="mwe_player_7" poster="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University%2C_September_12%2C_1962.ogv/220px-seek%3D1052-President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University%2C_September_12%2C_1962.ogv.jpg" controls="" preload="none" class="mw-file-element" width="220" height="164" data-durationhint="1068" data-mwtitle="President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University,_September_12,_1962.ogv" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons" resource="/wiki/File:President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University,_September_12,_1962.ogv"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/d0/President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University%2C_September_12%2C_1962.ogv/President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University%2C_September_12%2C_1962.ogv.240p.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp8, vorbis&quot;" data-title="Small WebM (240P)" data-shorttitle="WebM 240P" data-transcodekey="240p.webm" data-width="322" data-height="240" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/d0/President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University%2C_September_12%2C_1962.ogv/President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University%2C_September_12%2C_1962.ogv.240p.vp9.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp8, vorbis&quot;" data-title="Low bandwidth WebM (160P)" data-shorttitle="WebM 160P" data-transcodekey="160p.webm" data-width="214" data-height="160" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/d0/President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University%2C_September_12%2C_1962.ogv/President_Kennedy_speech_on_the_space_effort_at_Rice_University%2C_September_12%2C_1962.ogv.180p.vp9.webm" type="video/webm;
